title: Two Sibilants, One Liquid, and Three Standalone Vowels

lessons.title: ल — the plain l, beside the curled one you know
lessons.gloss: dental la — the plain l, partner to the retroflex lla you already write

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You learned the harder l first. Here is the ordinary one.
ल (la).
ल is plain la, the tongue at the teeth — the sound English writes with l. You already write ळ, the retroflex ḷ Marathi keeps alongside it, and which Hindi does not have at all.
Meeting the rare one first was not an accident: ळ sits in kāḷjī and ḍoḷā, words this book needed early. Now the common one arrives, and with it bolṇe, "to speak", becomes readable end to end.
Trace ल twice, then trace ळ once beside it. Say la and ḷa, moving the tongue back only for the second.
Which of the two does Hindi not have? (ळ.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari la stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Trace plain la, then name the Marathi letter for the curled l.

feedback.correct: Two l's, and Marathi keeps both.
feedback.incorrect: Repair only the shape, or only the name.

lessons.title: श (śa) — the sh at the roof of the mouth
lessons.gloss: palatal sha — the sh of shahar

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You write the plain s. Slide the tongue back along the roof of your mouth and it becomes something else.
श (śa).
श is śa, English sh. Marathi keeps it distinct from the स you learned in your first chapter, and the pair behaves like every other pair in this runway: same air, different place.

It opens śahar, "city" — one of the six labels the A1 form chapters will ask you to fill in. Draw the left hook, the upright, and the headline; the small loop at the top left is what separates it from म.
Copy श (śa) twice with the model visible. Then write स once beside it and say both, sliding the tongue back only for the first.
Which one opens śahar? (श.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari sha stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Copy palatal sha, then write plain sa from memory.

feedback.incorrect: Repair only the one that came out wrong.

lessons.title: ष (ṣa) — the third sibilant, kept on the page
lessons.gloss: retroflex sha — a third sibilant, written apart and mostly said like sha

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Marathi writes three sibilants and says two. This is the third one.
ष (ṣa).
ष is ṣa, the retroflex sibilant. Sanskrit distinguished it from श (śa); most Marathi speakers today say the two the same way, and keep them apart only in spelling.

That is worth knowing rather than hiding: a letter can survive in the writing system after the sound behind it has merged. ष (ṣa) appears in tatsama words taken whole from Sanskrit, such as bhāṣā, "language" — another of the six form labels waiting for you.
Look at ष (ṣa) for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside श (śa): two shapes your mouth no longer separates.
Are श (śa) and ष (ṣa) different sounds for most speakers today? (No — different spellings.)
Source: Opiaterein, Devanagari ssa stroke animation.

segments.prompt: Write retroflex sha after a delay, then say how most Marathi speakers pronounce it.

feedback.correct: A spelling distinction, named as one.
feedback.incorrect: Repair the shape, and keep the honest answer about the sound.

lessons.title: उ — short u standing on its own
lessons.gloss: independent short u — the vowel written whole when nothing carries it

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You already hang a short u under a consonant. What happens when there is no consonant to hang it on?
उ (u).
Then you write उ, the independent short u — the same vowel given its own full letter for the start of a word.

Devanagari does this for every vowel: a mark when something carries it, a letter when nothing does. You have already seen the pair once, with अ and its mark. उ opens udyā, "tomorrow", in the farewell this book taught you chapters ago.
Copy उ twice with the model visible. Then write the short-u mark beside it and say aloud which of the two needs a consonant to lean on.
Which word for tomorrow starts with it? (udyā.)
Source: Saurmandal, Devanagari u stroke order.

segments.prompt: Copy independent short u, then say which form needs a consonant to lean on.

feedback.correct: Letter when alone, mark when carried.
feedback.incorrect: Copy the full letter again, then name the leaning one.

lessons.gloss: independent long uu — the last sign of the second runway

needs: a pen and something to write on

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. segments.text: One more, and this runway is finished. It is the long partner of the letter you wrote a moment ago.
ऊ (ū).
ऊ is the independent long ū: उ (u) with a tail carried down and to the right, the same extra travel the long mark asked for below the line.
Four forms, one vowel: उ and ऊ (ū) when it stands alone, the short and long marks when a consonant carries it. That symmetry is the whole vowel system of this script, and you now write all of it.
Look at ऊ (ū) for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set the four u forms in a row: उ ऊ (ū) and the two marks. Repair only one.
How many written forms does this one vowel have? (Four.)
Source: Saurmandal, Devanagari uu stroke order.

segments.prompt: Write independent long uu after a delay, then name the four forms of this vowel.
acceptedResponses: ऊ; independent short, independent long, short matra, long matra

feedback.correct: The whole vowel, in all four of its forms.
feedback.incorrect: Repair the shape, or name the form you missed.

lessons.title: ए — the vowel that opens ek
lessons.gloss: independent long e — the vowel that opens ek, one

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: One vowel left, and you have been reading it since the chapter where you learned to count.
ए (e).
ए is the independent long e — the same vowel as the े mark you write above the headline, given its own letter for the start of a word.

It opens एक, ek, "one". That word has been printed beside its romanization since the counting chapter, which means you have been looking at this letter for a long time without being told what it was. Draw the left hook, the upright, and the headline; the mark version is what remains if you take the letter away and keep only the top.
Copy एक twice with the model visible, naming both signs: independent e, then ka. Then write the े mark once on its own and say which of the two forms needs a consonant to lean on.
Which number word starts with ए? (ek — one.)
Source: Saurmandal, Devanagari e stroke order.

segments.prompt: Copy ek, then say which form of this vowel needs a consonant to lean on.

feedback.correct: A word you have counted with for chapters is now a word you can write.
feedback.incorrect: Repair only the letter or only the mark, whichever slipped.

lessons.title: Twenty-four signs, at real distance
lessons.gloss: the whole second runway at distance — twenty-four signs across four chapters

segments.text: Four chapters ago the page was still full of shapes nobody had taught you. Close every model and find out what stayed.
Which l does Hindi not have? (The curled ळ.)
Which two sibilants are kept apart only in spelling? (śa and ṣa.)
How many written forms does the u vowel have? (Four — two letters and two marks.)
Which number word opens with the independent e? (ek.)
Which letter ends every infinitive? (ṇa.)
Which nasal mark wears a crescent? (The candrabindu.)
Which sign did mājhe need? (jha.)
And one from the chapter before: ba with the voice switched off? (pa, which is ba without the inner dot.)

segments.prompt: Name the plain l beside the curled one, the two sibilants Marathi writes apart and says alike, the three standalone vowels of this chapter, one letter from each of the three consonant rows in this runway, and ba with the voice switched off.
acceptedResponses: la beside lla; sha and ssa; u, uu and e; kha, jha, nna; pa

feedback.correct: The runway held: every row, both sibilants, and all four u forms.
feedback.incorrect: Repair one group only. A miss at this distance is information, not failure.
